title: Liars - Breaking and Entering
summary: Angus Andrew from Liars came into the studio to chat with Simon Winkler about their split 7" with TFS, and Angus' split with creative partner Aaron Hemphill.
transcript:
Angus Andrew of Liars joined Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio on 27 September 2018 to discuss Titles With The Word Fountain, his return to Australia and his latest collaborations. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: Liars began in America. You and Aaron Hemphill met in Los Angeles, moved to New York City and, in the early years of the millennium, became a core part of the Brooklyn warehouse scene alongside DFA Records, The Rapture and Yeah Yeah Yeahs. Over eighteen years, it's been a story of constant experimentation and innovation, moving across genres. Now you're back in your hometown of Melbourne, playing tonight, with an ACMI Wonderland Late Nights show tomorrow. You've marked the occasion with your Listening to Australia playlist. You've been away for quite some time, but you've been paying close attention to Australia's music scene.

Angus: I hadn't been, actually. It was only when I arrived back that I wanted to make a conscious decision to listen to more music. For most of the time I've been making music, I've really avoided listening to music. I get really easily influenced, so my solution has always been just to cut it all out, and that's been fine for me. But when I came back to Australia, I really wanted to know what was going on. I felt like I wanted to become part of the musical community, kind of. I started listening to the great radio stations here, which is a kind of unique thing in Australia that you don't come across in many other cities in the world, radio stations that play interesting and local artists. I found myself really interested, and thought, there are so many people I know around the world who don't know about this music I'm hearing. So I thought I'd try and make this continuous playlist of only Australian contemporary artists.

Simon: The playlist covers experimental rock, noise, electronic music, punk and more. You talked about isolating yourself from the music around you, but there's a physical side too. Following the 2014 album Mess, you and Aaron parted ways amicably. You returned to Australia to spend time with family, but also to isolate yourself creatively, in Ku-ring-gai National Park north of Sydney. Boats have become a big part of your life.

Angus: Yeah, you can't get there by car and there's no shops. I had to learn about boating, which has never been in my vocabulary, and tying knots. They have a great saying: if you don't know knots, tie lots. Tides have become a big factor because where I live, the tide can go out in a way where my boat gets beached, and then you are literally stranded. It's been interesting to get in connection with that. I mean, we could talk about the tide all day, because I still don't know how that works.

Simon: How do the tides fit into your days at the moment?

Angus: I have a tide app, and I plan my trips to the mainland, in quotes, around the tides, depending on whether the boat is beached. I can't get it out otherwise, because it's too heavy to lift. Sometimes I don't look at the app, plan something, run down to the water and go, oh, looks like I might be staying home today. You can always try the thing where I take my shoes off, roll the pants up and try to pull the boat out, but it never works. It's also a place where there's no mains water, so all our water is collected from the rain. As I'm sure you're aware, it's been a very dry year so far. When it rains, it's a really big event because we feel water-rich and can have a bath or something. I've never lived in a place so connected to the environment in that way, and I love it.

Simon: Each Liars album is very distinct from the last. I think you have a maxim that if you start to get too good at an instrument or method, you have to abandon it for future records, starting from scratch each time. How did moving from New York, Berlin and Los Angeles to the world you've described affect how you make music?

Angus: Even though I've been living in big cities, I've also pretty much isolated myself in those places. Living in Berlin, for example, I never learned to speak German, which is a horrible thing, but it allowed me the possibility of being on the train with everyone talking around me and not taking any of it in, which I really enjoyed. Moving here to the natural environment, what it did specifically, technically, was that the previous records I'd made in Los Angeles were quite rigid. I was using software to make music, and when you use software in a certain way it almost can write itself. It's to a grid, a time signature, and things can be very sharp. I was really interested in that at the time. But moving to the bush, I wanted everything to go off-time in this really beautiful way. When you're sitting in the bush and listening, there are repetitive sounds coming in and out. Sometimes they're connecting in a rhythm, but then they're not. The sound of the water with the wind in the trees, I was seeing these things in this time scale. I wanted my music to just fall apart in that way, in a much more organic way. But I was still interested in using the computer, so it was a question of how to achieve that. It was really by sampling myself playing the live instruments, then being able to manipulate them in different ways.

Simon: 'Double Elegy', from Titles With The Word Fountain, ends with granulated, ring-modulated synth sounds. The record comes from the TFCF deluxe edition and is a sequel in some ways to last year's album. You mentioned as we were playing it that the song features recordings from Melbourne.

Angus: I was here on a tour, I don't know how long ago, probably the last time I played in Melbourne. I had a day off and basically walked to all the old houses I used to live in. It was one of those great days where you're in a bit of a daze. Then I caught the tram back to where I was staying, a fairly long tram ride. I was sitting right behind this beautiful couple who talked freely the whole time, and I, of course, recorded them. I'd been sitting on this recording for so long, wanting to put it in the right place, and I'm glad there's a little bit there.

Simon: Elsewhere on the album are field recordings from your home in Ku-ring-gai. This album is closely related to TFCF, which came out last year. Could you talk about how they're connected?

Angus: In a practical sense, it was the label that was interested in doing a deluxe edition of TFCF. I'd delivered some B-sides, a few songs, which you always do when you deliver a record. They said, we're going to use these and do some remixes, and that'll be it. I remember sitting down and listening to those B-sides back to back and thinking, that's just not good enough. I knew I had so much material from that period of writing that I got to work bringing those things up to a level of releasement.

Simon: The technical term, correct?

Angus: Yeah, it's a technical term. And there it is. It's a big purge for me. It's nice to get the material written in that period all out in the world. Then I really feel like I can move on with my next project now.

Simon: You've said that as a project comes to an end, you become intrigued by its visual component, creating a world around it. What were your intentions for the visual world of this record?

Angus: When I make something, to get a sense of how it can work or how I might explain it to other people, it's helpful to go out into the bush and shoot video or photos. I'm often thinking, to be honest, in the context of other countries. My label is in London, and these people don't know this place. I'm trying to place the music in an environment, a way that people can realise where it's coming from. It also helps me understand it a bit better, and I really enjoy doing that. I began as a visual artist, really, and music only came after that, so I always go back to that.

Simon: You've spoken of your admiration for bands who are deliberately circuit-breaking in their practices. You've also said, I think in reference to Lawrence Weiner, that the artist's role is to instil an idea that's more important than the final object. Do you still subscribe to that?

Angus: I love that. My whole feeling about art is that it really happens more in the mind of the audience or the viewer. Their interpretation of whatever you're putting forward is, to me, just as valid as the intention. Lawrence Weiner is sort of the godfather of conceptual art, saying you really don't have to make the thing at all. If you could describe to the audience what you're thinking of making, in their minds they'll put it all together. What they put together is probably ten times more interesting than what you would have done, limited by the physics of life. I think it extends to all modes of art. It bleeds into stuff for me like lyrics too. For a long time I felt strongly about not printing lyrics, because I thought it was more interesting for the listener to interpret and find their own ideas of what I was saying. Then a few years down the track you come across someone on the internet who's written down what the lyrics are, and you're like, no. So I went through a period of printing the lyrics, and now I'm coming back around. That's what I do a lot, I flip-flop.

Simon: You revise.

Angus: Now I enjoy hearing interpretations.

Simon: I suppose trying to control the content on the internet is like trying to battle the tides.

Angus: Exactly, exactly.

Simon: You're in town for your first Melbourne tour in four years, performing tonight, Thursday 27 September, at The Curtin with Hexdebt and HTRK DJs, and tomorrow at ACMI Wonderland Late Nights. There's also the soundtrack to 'Liquorice'—

Angus: It's the soundtrack to 1/1.

Simon: 1/1, that's right. 'Liquorice' is the first taste of it. There's also a seven-inch out this week with Tropical Fuck Storm.

Angus: Can I use the cough button? Tropical Storm. Does that work?

Simon: First time the button's been used, as far as I can remember. What other projects do you have on the boil? Where will the tides take you next?

Angus: It's hard to say. Another thing that's been fun is working with two Australian musicians to put on these live shows, Laurence Pike and Cameron Deyell, who are genius musicians. It's been so fun to play with them. That's been going on. We did this split with TFS, and that came about suddenly, but it's always great when that happens. When something is a quick turnaround, it makes things much less inhibited. Having just released the last thing, I suppose I'm looking to next year to think of what I want to do. There are so many things exciting to me right now. I've been working with a Chinese company, a really big music company there, who haven't expanded much outside China and are interested in doing that. I've been trying to tell them about some great Australian artists they should sign and bring over there. It's an interesting place. I did a tour there recently and, as they say in all parts of the economy, there's a lot of room for growth there for music. That's an exciting thing.

Simon: It's been a privilege to hear what's happening in your world, and what's ahead as a participant and ambassador for Australian music.

Angus: Thank you.
